item.title: Standing to one side, the deity Candana recited this verse to the Blessed One: How can one cross the flood, Steadfast and persevering day and…
item.description:
Standing to one side, the deity Candana recited this verse to the Blessed One:
How can one cross the flood,
Steadfast and persevering day and night?
Without stalling, without clinging —
Who does not sink in the abyss?

(The Blessed One):
One who always has virtue,
Wisdom, and is well-concentrated,
With aroused energy and strength —
That one crosses the hard-to-cross flood.
One who has abandoned perception of lust,
Who has crossed beyond the fetter of form,
Who has destroyed delight and craving for existence —
That one does not sink in the abyss.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.15

item.title: “Monks, how does a monk live as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island,…
item.description:
“Monks, how does a monk live as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge? Monks, here a monk abides contemplating the body as a body internally, ardent, diligent, mindful, clearly comprehending, to remove covetousness and sorrow in the world; abides contemplating feelings as feelings … mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, ardent, diligent, mindful, clearly comprehending, to remove covetousness and sorrow in the world. Thus, monks, a monk lives as an island unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, seeking no other refuge.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 26 – Cakkavattisutta

item.title: “Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he…
item.description:
“Monks, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding this body composed of the four great elements. Why is that? Because he sees this body composed of the four great elements increasing and decreasing, being taken up and discarded. Therefore, an untaught ordinary person might become disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated regarding it. But regarding that which is called mind, intellect, consciousness — here, an untaught ordinary person is not capable of disenchantment, not capable of dispassion, not capable of liberation. Why is that? For a long time, monks, an untaught ordinary person has been attached, regarded as ‘mine,’ grasped at: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self.’ Therefore, he is not capable of disenchantment, dispassion, or liberation regarding it.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.61

item.title: “And when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements — sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt — then it…
item.description:
“And when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements — sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt — then it becomes malleable, wieldy, radiant, not brittle, properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. Regarding whatever state is to be directly known, the mind inclines to direct knowledge, and in each case he attains the ability and capacity to realize that state.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.23

item.title: “Vāseṭṭha, there are five factors that cause the growth of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye — desirable, beautiful, delightful, enticing, connected…
item.description:
“Vāseṭṭha, there are five factors that cause the growth of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye — desirable, beautiful, delightful, enticing, connected with sensual pleasure and enjoyment; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … touches cognizable by the body — desirable, beautiful, delightful, enticing, connected with sensual pleasure and enjoyment. Vāseṭṭha, those five factors that cause the growth of sensual pleasure — the brahmins proficient in the three Vedas, attached, infatuated, bound, not seeing their danger, not understanding the escape from them, enjoy them. Vāseṭṭha, that those brahmins proficient in the three Vedas, abandoning the qualities that make a brahmin, following qualities that do not make a brahmin, attached, infatuated, bound, not seeing their danger, not understanding the escape from them, enjoying them, bound by the bondage of sensual pleasures, could after death be reborn in union with Brahmā — such a thing is not possible.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 13 – Tevijjasutta

item.title: "O great king, when the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes…
item.description:
"O great king, when the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the eye faculty, practices the restraint of the eye faculty."

From: Dīgha Nikāya 2 – Sāmaññaphalasutta

item.title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future? Monks, there are some ascetics…
item.description:
“Monks, what is a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future? Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine, such a view: ‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures.’ They indulge in sensual pleasures. Having indulged, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a plane of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. There they experience painful, sharp, severe feelings. They say: ‘Those venerable ascetics and brahmins who see the future danger in sensual pleasures, who speak of the abandoning of sensual pleasures, who describe the full understanding of sensual pleasures—but we, with these sensual pleasures as the cause, as the condition, experience these painful, sharp, severe feelings.’ Monks, this is called a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 45 – Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta

item.title: “Cut down the forest, not just a tree — From the forest, fear is born. Having cut down both forest and undergrowth, Be forest-free, O…
item.description:
“Cut down the forest, not just a tree —
From the forest, fear is born.
Having cut down both forest and undergrowth,
Be forest-free, O monks.”

“As long as even the smallest desire
Of a man for women is not cut off,
His mind is bound like a suckling calf to its mother.”

“Cut off your affection,
Like plucking an autumn lotus with the hand.
Develop the path to peace, Nibbāna,
Taught by the Well-gone One.”

From: Dhammapada 273-289

item.title: “Venerable sirs, what is the effort of abandoning? Here, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent.…
item.description:
“Venerable sirs, what is the effort of abandoning? Here, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to arisen ill-will thought … he does not consent to arisen harmful thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. This, venerable sirs, is called the effort of abandoning.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 33 – Saṅgītisutta

item.title: “Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises…
item.description:
“Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — because of that, delight arises. Migajāla, I say that with the arising of delight, suffering arises. Sounds … Odors … Tastes … Touches … Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk delights in them, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — because of that, delight arises. Migajāla, I say that with the arising of delight, suffering arises.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.64
